blocks.speaker: SPEAKER_00
blocks.text: good evening my name is chris balke hilditch i'm deputy director of public works for the city of lancaster for utilities with me is my co-worker ben perwin he's the senior project manager in our water bureau this evening we're here to present the environmental review for our phase two and phase three large diameter transmission made we will go over the permitting that's been involved in this project and we'll talk about why there's a public meeting about this under the national environmental policy and we'll also review the timeline of the project

blocks.speaker: SPEAKER_01
blocks.text: so what is the phase two and three large diameter transmission main project a little bit of a back story in the way that the city actually produces water the city of lancaster owns operates and maintains a potable water system that provides water to over 120 000 people in lancaster county the system is supplied from two water treatment plants one that is fed from the conestoga river and one that is read from the susquehanna river the susquehanna treatment plant was built in the 1950s and while the treatment plant and pumping infrastructure have all been upgraded the pipes going from the river intake to the treatment plant and then from the treatment plant and then the finished water from the treatment plant to the reservoir and then into the city were not touched in 2012 there was a leak on this line and it cost about two hundred thousand dollars to fix the city was able to keep water flowing throughout this time however it was a little bit of wake-up call to us that says that we needed better infrastructure so that this wouldn't be an issue in the future a study came out of this and laid the groundwork for this project i have been involved in i have been with the city for about 12 years and this project has been with me this entire 12 years the study came out in 2020 in 2013 and we've been working on it ever since in 2022 the city finished phase one of the large diameter transmission main which completed the main which completed a redundant main from the treatment from our oyster point reservoir into the city so this would just be finishing that project and adding a redundant line to the main that was installed in 1955. This map shows the proposed route of the water main that is proposed. The orange line is the phase three large diameter transmission main and that is the raw water line from the river to the treatment plant. Phase two is the treated water that goes from the treatment plant up to our oyster point reservoir you can see in mountville there is a line that goes up this provides an interconnect to one of our um to one of our other distribution mains and it allows the city's distribution network to have full redundancy this main runs through Columbia Borough, West Hemfield, Mount Ville Borough, and into East Hemfield. These are some of the just the required permits that we were that we needed to get for this project. There are many different acronym organizations that were used that provide these permits. The first two permits are from the PADP, Safe Drinking Water Bureau. They have one for the the raw water phase and one for the finished water phase this main also crosses two different railroads one being norfolk southern and the other one being the columbia and reading railroad there's a 10 dot highway occupancy permit that's required because some of this main goes along columbia avenue and route 462 and then there's many other local road permits that we would need to get. NPDS permit is stands for the National Palloon Discharge and it is required for when you're disturbing the earth and so that we don't have any issues with the environment while we're doing the construction of this. And then the last permit is the joint permit for the stream crossings. These are joint responsibility between the PADP and the Army Corps and the Army Corps of Engineers. All these permits have been applied for and we're working on getting them and we're working through comments currently.

Our project cost for the project is estimated between 40 and 50 million and this includes approximately 1.25 million of design and surveying services. The city applied to the Commonwealth Finance Authority for ARPA funding in 2023 for the full cost of both projects, both phase two and phase three, but only received $3,132,000 for phase two. There was significant competition for the ARPA funding throughout the entire state of Pennsylvania. we are applying for pen best funding pen best is a gives us low interest loans to utilities in the commonwealth and one of the requirements that they have is that they require that any major project have an environmental study under the national environmental policy and we'll hear the acronym nipa nipa establishes the national charter for environmental protection it requires the identification of environmental consequences and mitigation measures so even though we have multiple permits that we've applied for because of those permits specifically some of our project will be in the flood plain and that's unavoidable because we have to withdraw water from the susquehanna river so we're in the floodplain being adjacent to the river and as ben pointed out we have several stream crossings to get the water throughout the distribution system under this environmental policy there's three different tiers of environmental review the first one being a categorical exclusion an environmental assessment and then a very full-scale project review an environmental impact statement the eis was not required for this project the city had applied for the categorical exclusion but dep had ruled that we were not allowed to do that because of the creek crossings and the and the floodplain impact so the categorical exclusion is only used for projects with no significant impact and again as i said the project was not eligible because of the creek crossings and the floodplain some examples of eligible projects that we've been successful with in the past inflow and infiltration correction in wastewater systems cleaning and lining of drinking water pipes repair of existing equipment these are types of projects where we would not be disturbing anything in the environment an example of those where we are disturbing might be new or relocated wastewater discharges intakes or substantial increases in discharge fall so where we ended up falling was under the environmental assessment so this is the next stage for projects not eligible for a categorical exclusion so since we were not eligible we started under this path we are utilizing a process called the uniform environmental process or uer and this is what was required by the padep and penbase the city hired arrow engineering to do an environmental assessment the plans are now completed and they're working through the narratives now with the in preparation for filing with the dep one of the requirements is that we have the ability to talk about our project before the public so we're on youtube this evening to allow the public to understand this project and to ask questions in the future so this is why we're here this
